text: Larkspur wants to extend SupportPilot with two new tools, close_ticket and issue_refund, and its security team requires every AI feature to pass a written review before it ships. This lab builds that checklist from the ground up, using the five categories that map back to this course's earlier chapters -- not a vague gut-check, but specific, checkable items.

The first two categories come straight from Chapter 2 and Chapter 3: every retrieval source gets labeled trusted or untrusted, retrieved content is marked as data rather than instructions, and Lesson 29's marker-string test gets run against every untrusted source. Data and model provenance get documented the same way, so nothing ships on an unexamined source.

Category 5, architecture, is where Lesson 29's finding becomes an actual gate instead of a one-off fix. Privilege separation means close_ticket and issue_refund are distinct, narrowly-scoped tools -- a summarization call can never also trigger a refund. A human approval gate sits in front of anything with real-world effect, and secrets stay out of the model's own context entirely.

All five categories feed one go or no-go gate: a short form with a pass or fail per category and a single overall decision, ship or do not ship. That's deliberately binary -- it ties the outcome to specific checked items instead of a reviewer's subjective comfort level, the same role a pen-test sign-off plays for any other feature.

Applied to issue_refund directly, the gate requires both halves of the fix: marking retrieved ticket content as untrusted data, and putting a human approval step in front of the refund call itself. Passing only one still leaves a real path open -- either an injection that still can't be stopped by the gate, or a gate that still lets unmarked, untrusted content drive it.

A checklist that only catches the injection but still lets the agent refund money autonomously hasn't actually closed the risk, and neither has an approval gate sitting behind a prompt template that still treats attacker-controlled text as instructions. Lesson 31's case study shows exactly what happens when a feature ships with only one of those two gates in place.
